evaluated.name: LeveredTurnaroundTrend
evaluated.hypothesis: An improving operating profitability trajectory is most valuable — and most underappreciated — for highly levered firms, where a rising trend mechanically reduces default probability and transfers value from creditors to equity; the same trend in an unlevered firm carries little option value.
evaluated.reasoning: TREND over five years captures the direction of the profitability state rather than its level, which is the variable that resolves distress uncertainty, and the leverage rank scales the payoff so that deteriorating levered firms sit at the short end. This is a genuine interaction because the trend's return relevance is conditioned on the distress state, not on profitability alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeverageWeightedGrossProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, ADD(cogs, xsga)), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Because equity is a residual claim, one unit of operating profitability moves equity value far more when the firm carries heavy liabilities and a thin working-capital buffer; investors underreact to this leverage-amplified information, so profitability earns its largest premium exactly where distress exposure is greatest.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique was that a z-scored leverage multiplier flips sign for low-leverage firms and pooled unprofitable-unlevered names into the long leg; replacing it with a strictly non-negative distress weight (rank of a leverage plus working-capital-deficiency composite in [0,1]) makes the signal monotone in profitability at every leverage level and near zero for the safest firms. The long leg is therefore unambiguously profitable-and-stressed and the short leg unprofitable-and-stressed, which is the interaction the hypothesis describes rather than either main effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorstCaseObligationCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Default is triggered by the trough of operating earnings, not their average, so the distress-relevant quantity is the firm's worst recent operating profit relative to its total obligations; markets extrapolate mean profitability and therefore underprice firms whose downside profitability still covers their liability stock.
evaluated.reasoning: This is no longer the inverse of net-debt/EBITDA: the numerator is a left-tail (three-year minimum) profitability state rather than a level or smoothed mean, which is a genuinely distress-conditioned way of measuring profitability. Scaling by total liabilities instead of interest-bearing debt removes the exploding-denominator fragility for zero-debt firms, since every firm has non-trivial liabilities, so winsorization is a mild guard rather than the source of the signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OperatingFinancialDoubleLeverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Fixed-cost intensity (depreciation per unit of sales) amplifies the earnings sensitivity of a downturn, and when it is stacked on top of financial leverage the compounded operating-plus-financial risk is systematically underestimated, so double-levered firms subsequently underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests the cost-structure side of profitability rather than its level, giving an interaction the archive has not touched: the same debt load is much more dangerous for a firm whose margins cannot flex. The signed industry-rank z-score for operating leverage keeps both legs populated (capital-light levered firms are long, capital-heavy levered firms are short) and the leverage rank mutes debt-free firms where operating leverage is not a distress channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FlowVersusStockSolvencyGap
evaluated.hypothesis: Balance-sheet leverage and earnings-based interest coverage classify distress differently, and investors (like credit screens and index filters) anchor on the visible stock measure; firms that look highly levered but whose operating profit easily services their interest burden are misclassified as risky and are therefore underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the profitability × leverage-rank product family entirely and instead prices the *disagreement* between a flow-based (profit-to-interest) and a stock-based (liabilities-to-assets) distress classification, which is neither the gross-profitability premium nor a leverage sort. Both channels enter as bounded industry ranks so the long leg is coherently "levered but comfortably covered" and the short leg is "low-book-leverage but interest-strained," with neither theme able to drive the spread alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ObligationGrowthOutpacingProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is built, not inherited: when a firm's liabilities expand faster than its operating earning power, the incremental obligations are not self-financing and future default risk rises, yet the market treats liability-funded expansion as growth rather than as deteriorating solvency capacity.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than swapping the denominator of the archived coverage ratio, this compares the *flows* of the two themes — asset-scaled liability accumulation versus asset-scaled profit accumulation — so the signal is high only when obligations grow without matching profit support, an imbalance neither a leverage level nor a profit-change sort captures. Using asset-scaled first differences instead of growth rates avoids the exploding ratios that plague GROWTH(oibdp) for firms with near-zero or negative base earnings.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashRunwayForWeakEarners
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquidity buffers are priced asymmetrically: for firms with weak operating profitability, cash relative to total liabilities is the survival runway that determines whether distress is realized, whereas for already-profitable firms the same cash is idle balance-sheet slack that earns no premium and may signal agency costs.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the trivial ΔROA-to-liabilities idea with a genuine state-contingent liquidity mechanism, testing whether the cash cushion offsets weak profitability — the "offsets" leg of the task's economic story that the archive has not probed. The profitability term is a centered bounded rank z-score, so the long leg is weak-earner/high-cash and the short leg is strong-earner/high-cash, with cash-poor firms concentrated near zero rather than at an extreme.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CenteredEarningsRiskUnderLeverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Default probability is driven by the product of cash-flow volatility and obligation size, so among levered firms earnings instability should be penalized sharply while among unlevered firms it should be nearly irrelevant; the market applies a roughly uniform volatility discount and therefore misprices the interaction.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique was correct that a non-negative VOL times a non-negative leverage rank, then negated, ranks unlevered firms at the top; centering the volatility input as an industry-rank z-score fixes the ordering so that stable levered firms occupy the long leg, volatile levered firms the short leg, and debt-free firms sit in the middle. This makes the tested quantity the leverage-conditional slope on earnings risk rather than the level of earnings volatility itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OverheadRetrenchmentUnderDebt
evaluated.hypothesis: Levered firms have no slack to absorb rising overhead: a falling SG&A-to-sales ratio credibly restores debt-service capacity and lowers default risk, while overhead creep at a levered firm is an early, under-monitored sign of margin erosion that will meet a hard obligation constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: This swaps the discredited book-tax-difference channel for a cost-discipline channel: the change in overhead intensity is only distress-relevant when obligations are large, which is a conditioning claim rather than a restatement of any cost-stickiness or profitability anomaly. The centered rank z-score of the overhead change keeps both legs populated among levered firms and mutes debt-free firms, where SG&A drift carries no solvency implication.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LenderRateVersusReportedProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: The effective interest rate a firm pays embeds private lender information about default risk; when accounting profitability looks healthy, equity investors are complacent and ignore this credit-market warning, so a high lender-imposed rate predicts low returns most strongly among apparently profitable firms.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces an external, price-based distress measure rather than another balance-sheet ratio, and conditions it on profitability, so the tested claim is that credit-market and accounting signals conflict and the credit market wins. The signed carrier is the industry-standardized borrowing rate (raw-ratio IND_ZSCORE, which evaluates reliably) while the non-negative profitability rank mutes unprofitable firms, where the equity market is already alert to distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SolvencyMarginOwnHistoryPosition
evaluated.hypothesis: Credit quality is judged relative to a firm's own history: when operating profit per unit of obligations sits near the top of its five-year range, default risk has fallen materially from the level embedded in prices, and this within-firm improvement is absorbed more slowly than the cross-sectional level.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the reference frame rather than the ingredients — position in own history instead of position in the cross-section — which separates firm-specific credit-quality improvement from persistent industry or size effects that a cross-sectional coverage sort inherits. It is parsimonious, uses only oibdp and lt so coverage should exceed the TS_MIN-based winner, and provides a clean read on whether the coverage effect is a level or a within-firm-change phenomenon.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsDrawdownUnderObligations
evaluated.hypothesis: Distance below peak earning power measures proximity to covenant breach and refinancing failure, and this drawdown is dangerous only when obligations are large; markets extrapolate the current earnings level and underweight how far a levered firm has fallen from the cash-flow base its debt was raised against.
evaluated.reasoning: Peak-to-current earnings drawdown is a distinct temporal concept from the archive's trend and level signals — it captures crisis proximity rather than direction or average — and interacting it with leverage is exactly the state dependence the mandate asks for. Centering the drawdown with IND_ZSCORE (not a non-negative magnitude) fixes the ordering flaw the critic identified in gen 1, so at-peak levered firms are long, deeply drawn-down levered firms are short, and debt-free firms sit near the middle.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginCompressionUnderObligations
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising unit cost of sales erodes the cash flow pledged against fixed claims, so gross-margin compression is a leading indicator of default risk only for obligation-heavy firms; the market reads margin drift as an operating detail and misses its solvency implication where there is no slack to absorb it.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the net-debt-issuance-adjacent flow diagnostic with a cost-side margin channel that no archived signal touches, and it conditions on obligations rather than adding another debt-growth leg. The signed carrier is the centered change in cost intensity and the weight is a non-negative leverage rank, so improving-margin levered firms are long, compressing-margin levered firms are short, and debt-free firms sit near the middle; coverage should be high since only cogs, sale, lt and at are required.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CurrentProfitVersusLossHistory
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors anchor distress assessments on a firm's accumulated earnings record — the retained-earnings deficit that credit models weight heavily — and are slow to recognize when current operating profitability has already recovered; the gap between present earning power and the accumulated record is therefore underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new economic claim rather than a blend of archived signals: it prices the *disagreement between stock and flow measures of profitability*, where the stock version (retained earnings to assets) is the classic accumulated-distress state variable and the flow version is current earning power. The rank-difference structure has evaluated cleanly in this environment, keeps both legs populated (long = recovering deficit firms, short = firms coasting on past earnings with weak current profit), and requires only oibdp, re and at so coverage should exceed the TS_MIN family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FloatFinancedProfitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Negative working capital is a standard distress marker, but for firms with strong gross margins it instead reflects supplier and customer float — a cheap, self-renewing funding source — so the market over-penalizes working-capital deficiency among profitable firms and those firms subsequently outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-proposing cash-versus-profitability, this tests the opposite sign convention on a different distress dimension: whether profitability *reinterprets* a liquidity-deficiency signal instead of merely offsetting it. The centered working-capital carrier and non-negative gross-profitability weight put float-financed profitable operators in the long leg and working-capital-heavy profitable firms in the short leg, while unprofitable firms — where the deficiency is genuine distress — are muted near zero.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RolloverPressureAgainstProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: If the working-capital result is really about near-term funding risk, the active ingredient should be current debt rather than the full act−lct netting: profitable firms carrying heavy short-maturity debt must repeatedly return to credit markets, and that rollover exposure is not compensated in equity prices.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes Signal 1's mechanism by isolating the maturity-structure component of the liability side, so the pair jointly identifies whether the effect is a liquid-asset buffer story or a short-term-obligation story — an attribution the archive cannot currently make. The construction (centered distress carrier × non-negative profitability rank) is the one that has evaluated cleanly and keeps unprofitable firms muted, where rollover risk is already visibly priced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtServiceableCashAfterWorkingCapital
evaluated.hypothesis: Operating profit overstates the cash actually available to service obligations because growth in working capital absorbs it; the distress-relevant quantity is profit net of working-capital investment relative to total liabilities, and firms whose reported profitability is not truly available for debt service are overvalued.
evaluated.reasoning: This keeps the winning obligation-coverage frame but changes its economic content: the numerator is free cash available for fixed claims rather than accounting profit, so the signal separates firms whose earnings genuinely reduce default risk from those whose earnings are trapped in receivables and inventory. It uses only oibdp, wcap and lt, so coverage should match or exceed the TS_MIN-based winner while adding a cash-conversion dimension the archive lacks.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReplacementBurdenOnLeveredEarnings
evaluated.hypothesis: EBITDA overstates the cash genuinely available to service fixed claims when a large fraction of it must be reinvested to replace depreciating assets; for obligation-heavy firms this replacement burden is a hidden claim ahead of debt service, so levered firms whose earnings are mostly depreciation charges are riskier than their coverage ratios suggest.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new economic channel rather than a re-signed duplicate: it asks how much of operating profit is economically committed to asset replacement, complementing the accepted working-capital-drain measure with the fixed-asset drain, and it is only distress-relevant where obligations are large. The centered, winsorized carrier keeps both legs populated among levered firms (long = low replacement burden, short = depreciation-heavy) and mutes debt-free firms; it needs only dp, oibdp, lt and at, all high-coverage items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CostRigidityUnderObligations
evaluated.hypothesis: A cost base dominated by fixed overhead rather than variable production cost cannot be shrunk when demand falls, so overhead-rigid firms convert a revenue shock into a solvency event; this fragility matters only when obligations are large, and the market prices cost structure as an operating characteristic rather than a distress amplifier.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the flagged proposal this changes the profitability channel itself — cost *composition* (a state) rather than cost *change* (a flow) — so it tests a distinct fragility mechanism instead of retuning the conditioning state, and it avoids che entirely so coverage risk is limited to xsga reporting. Among levered firms the long leg is variable-cost-flexible operators and the short leg is overhead-rigid ones, with unlevered firms muted where cost rigidity carries no default implication.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReturnMinusBorrowingCostSpread
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency dynamics are governed by whether a firm's operating return exceeds the rate its lenders charge: a positive spread makes leverage self-liquidating and default risk mean-reverting downward, while a negative spread means debt compounds faster than earnings, and the market does not fully impound this comparison.
evaluated.reasoning: Instead of relabelling the sign on the archived conditional product, this builds a different construct — the spread between asset return and lender-imposed borrowing cost — which makes an explicit directional claim testable in both the FMB slope and the portfolio legs rather than fitting one to the other. The rank-difference form bounds the badly behaved low-debt tail of the borrowing-rate ratio (further winsorized) and keeps both legs economically interpretable: long = earns more than it pays, short = pays more than it earns.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MaturityMixAgainstProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes profitability valuable is not the amount of debt but how soon it must be repaid: profitable firms that have termed out their borrowing are insulated from credit-market closures, while profitable firms funding themselves at the short end are exposed to rollover risk that equity prices do not discount.
evaluated.reasoning: This holds leverage quantity fixed and varies only the maturity mix, so it separates the winner's mechanism (rollover exposure) from a simple scaled-debt effect, which the archive cannot currently distinguish because dlc/at mixes both. If the maturity-share version retains the fmb ≈ 3.9 / alpha ≈ 4% profile, the mechanism is genuinely refinancing risk; if it collapses, the winner was about debt quantity and the modulator was doing the work.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency at the relevant horizon is whether one year of gross profit can retire the claims that actually come due; firms whose near-term obligations are small relative to their gross profit flow face negligible refinancing risk and are underpriced relative to that safety.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether the multiplicative conditional structure is necessary at all, or whether directly scaling profitability by *near-term* obligations captures the same economics more robustly — the level analogue of the winner, and a sharper version of WorstCaseObligationCoverage (which used total liabilities and delivered 2.61 / +1.7%). It is parsimonious, uses only revt, cogs and lct, and its comparison with Signal 1 pins down whether the effect is coverage-level or conditional-slope in nature.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RolloverShockAgainstProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: A profitable firm that is suddenly shifting its funding to the short end is being rationed by long-term lenders, so the *increase* in current-debt intensity is a live warning of financing stress that the market reads as ordinary working-capital borrowing.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the winner from a state to a flow, which distinguishes a persistent capital-structure characteristic (possibly a risk-premium story spanned by known maturity effects) from a genuine news-based mispricing about deteriorating credit access. The design is deliberately identical in every other respect so the level-versus-change comparison is clean, and coverage should be close to 0.14 since only one lag is added.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RepairedEarningsRiskUnderObligations
evaluated.hypothesis: Default probability rises with the product of cash-flow volatility and obligation size, so earnings instability should be penalized sharply among obligation-heavy firms and be nearly irrelevant for debt-light firms; a market that applies a uniform volatility discount misprices this interaction.
evaluated.reasoning: This second-moment channel has never actually been tested — its gen-1 version returned 0% coverage purely because of the ZSCORE(IND_RANK) construction bug — and it is the one distress input orthogonal to every level, change and drawdown measure in the archive. Written with IND_ZSCORE of the raw volatility it should evaluate at coverage comparable to the other five-year-window signals (≈0.12–0.14), with stable levered earners long and volatile levered earners short.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitPremiumInDeficitFirms
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms carrying accumulated retained-earnings deficits are priced as chronic distress cases regardless of current performance, so the operating-profitability premium should be strongest exactly there, where profitability is the variable that resolves survival, and weakest among firms whose long earnings record already reassures investors.
evaluated.reasoning: CurrentProfitVersusLossHistory (alpha +1.8%, t 2.10) showed the current-versus-cumulative profitability gap is priced, but a rank difference cannot say whether the effect is a genuine conditional slope or just two additive channels; this multiplicative form isolates the interaction by muting firms with strong retained earnings. It uses only oibdp, re and at, so coverage should stay near 0.14, and it delivers a lesson that none of the rollover-family signals in this batch can provide.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OperatingCycleVelocityUnderNearTermClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm meets claims that come due out of the cash its operating cycle throws off, so the speed at which current assets convert into cash — cost of goods sold per dollar of current assets — is distress insurance precisely for firms whose balance sheets are loaded with near-term liabilities; slow-turning inventory and receivables cannot be converted on demand, making an otherwise identical claim load far more dangerous.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new economic channel rather than a re-signed prior: it prices the *velocity* of the operating cycle against the timing of obligations, whereas every archived signal uses profitability levels, changes, second moments, or obligation quantities. The signed carrier (industry-centered, winsorized turnover of current assets) is modulated by a non-negative current-liability rank, so fast-converting claim-heavy firms are long, slow-converting claim-heavy firms are short, and firms with negligible near-term claims sit near the middle where conversion speed has no solvency content; coverage should be high since cogs, act and lct are all standard items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HardVersusSoftNearTermClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all claims due within a year are equally dangerous: bank and market debt is a hard claim whose non-payment triggers default, whereas payables and accruals are soft claims that roll with ongoing supplier relationships, so for profitable firms it is the *hardness* of near-term claims, not their quantity, that determines true distress risk.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a genuinely new claim about claim quality — orthogonal to quantity (dlc/at), maturity mix (dlc/(dltt+dlc)) and coverage (gp/lct) — and it discriminates a trade-credit story from a default-trigger story, which the archive cannot currently do. If hardness is what matters, this should match or beat the winner; if the effect is really about total near-term claim size, it will weaken, which is itself decisive information for the remaining generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RolloverRiskAtHighCreditCost
evaluated.hypothesis: Short-maturity debt is dangerous in proportion to how expensive the firm's marginal credit already is: when lenders charge a high effective rate they are signalling limited willingness to refinance, so rollover exposure and a high borrowing cost compound into genuine default risk, whereas cheap borrowers can roll short debt at will.
evaluated.reasoning: Instead of averaging two archived carriers, this replaces the modulator with a *credit-market-implied* quality measure, so the tested claim is that rollover risk is priced only where lenders have already flagged the firm — an interaction between the quantity and the price of near-term credit that the archive has never combined. The centered current-debt carrier keeps both legs populated within the expensive-borrower group, and the winsorized rate addresses the low-debt instability the critic previously noted.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PostInterestProfitCoverageOfClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash genuinely available to retire claims coming due is operating profit *after* the contractual interest charge, since interest is senior to principal repayment; firms whose near-term claims are small relative to post-interest profit have real repayment capacity, while gross or pre-interest measures overstate the cushion of heavily indebted firms.
evaluated.reasoning: This removes the accounting linkage the critic identified — there is no Δwcap term, so the numerator is not mechanically tied to lct — and it adds economic content that no archived coverage ratio has: seniority, by subtracting the fixed charge before measuring the cushion. It therefore discriminates whether the near-term coverage alpha comes from operating scale (gross profit) or from the residual after fixed claims, using only high-coverage items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitPersistenceOffsetsRolloverRisk
evaluated.hypothesis: Lenders and investors distinguish poorly between firms that have earned operating profits every year and firms that earn them intermittently, yet only the former can reliably roll short-maturity debt; profit *persistence* therefore offsets rollover risk, and its value is concentrated among firms with heavy current debt.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a genuinely different profitability construct — a five-year count of profitable years, not a level, change, trough or second moment — and it directly implements the mandate's "profitability offsets distress" channel on the near-term claim dimension that the archive has shown to matter. The count is centered by industry so both legs are populated among short-debt-heavy firms (long = consistently profitable, short = intermittently profitable), and unlevered-at-the-short-end firms are muted.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitRetainedAsLossAbsorbingCapital
evaluated.hypothesis: Profits only reduce default risk if they are kept inside the firm: the share of gross profit that converts into retained earnings measures internal capital formation, and firms converting a large fraction into loss-absorbing equity are becoming structurally safer in a way the market does not price, while firms whose profits leak out as payouts or charges are not.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new economic quantity rather than an input substitution: it links the profitability flow to the distress state variable through a *conversion rate*, testing whether profit that becomes equity capital is what matters rather than profit itself. The gross-profit denominator is almost always positive, so the ratio is well behaved without needing rank machinery, and it uses only re, revt and cogs so coverage should be near the archive's best.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnstableNearTermSafetyMargin
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for refinancing is not only the average size of the safety margin but its reliability: a firm whose gross-profit-to-current-claims ratio swings widely can find itself uncovered exactly when credit tightens, so instability in the coverage margin is a distress characteristic distinct from its level.
evaluated.reasoning: This measures the second moment of the cross-theme coverage margin itself, which is not a smoothing variant of any archived signal but a different statistic with a different economic claim — margin uncertainty rather than margin size — and it is orthogonal to the level ratio that already scores well. Industry-centering makes the sort comparable across sectors with different working-capital cycles, and the five-year window puts expected coverage near 0.12, in line with other window-based signals in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetHardClaimShareAgainstProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), lct))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash on the balance sheet can extinguish maturing debt on demand, so the true hard-claim burden is short-term debt net of cash; a profitable firm whose cash already covers its maturing debt bears no refinancing risk at all, while one whose net hard claims dominate its near-term liabilities is exposed regardless of reported profits.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an economically substantive sharpening of the archive's best carrier (dlc/lct, fmb 4.15, α +4.0%), not a deflator swap: it recognizes that the relevant object is the *net* hard claim, which should push firms with large cash balances out of the short leg where they do not belong. The modulator and construction are held fixed so the test is a clean read on whether cash netting adds information to the hard-claim share.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueScaleCoverageControl
evaluated.hypothesis: If the near-term coverage effect is genuinely about profitability offsetting distress, then replacing gross profit with revenue — same claims denominator, no margin content — should weaken the result substantially; if instead pure operating scale relative to maturing claims does the work, the discovery is a turnover effect rather than a profitability × distress interaction.
evaluated.reasoning: GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims delivers fmb 3.25 and α +3.8%, but the critic correctly noted it is gross profitability times inverse short-liability intensity, and nothing in the archive separates the margin channel from the scale channel. This control is cheap, high-coverage and decisive for how the last generations should allocate effort, and it remains a legitimate cross-theme signal in its own right.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NearTermResourceShortfall
evaluated.hypothesis: Default is a shortfall event: what matters is whether claims coming due exceed the sum of the firm's liquid reserves and the gross profit its operations will generate over the year, and firms running such a shortfall must obtain external funding on whatever terms the market offers.
evaluated.reasoning: This expresses the same economics as the coverage ratios but as a size-scaled *difference* rather than a quotient, which changes what the extreme portfolios contain — ratios put tiny-denominator firms in the tails, while a shortfall scaled by assets puts genuinely under-resourced firms there — and it is the first construct in the archive to combine liquid reserves and the profit flow against claims in one balance. Its comparison with Signals 1–3 tells us whether the alpha is a coverage-ranking artifact or a real funding-gap effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AdditiveProfitVersusHardClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: If the profitability and hard-claim channels enter returns additively, a rank difference should capture the effect as well as the product; if the effect is genuinely conditional — profitability mattering more where hard claims are heavy and vice versa — the multiplicative form should dominate.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's strongest result uses a multiplicative structure but has never been benchmarked against the additive combination of the identical ingredients, so this isolates operator structure alone and directly tests whether the interaction claim is doing economic work. Rank differences have evaluated cleanly here (ObligationGrowthOutpacingProfit reached |t| 4.15 in FMB), so the comparison is fair rather than handicapped by construction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnconditionalCashCoverageWithProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: Only cash is liquid when credit closes: receivables and inventory cannot be monetized on demand precisely in the states where claims must be settled, so for profitable firms it is cash relative to maturing claims — not total current assets — that eliminates rollover dependence, and the market prices the two forms of liquidity alike.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash is a small and highly skewed component of current assets, so che/lct is not a monotone transform of wcap/at or act/lct and is not the archive's reversal re-run; it makes a sharper economic claim about *which* liquid resources are distress-relevant. Paired with the accepted net-hard-claim signal, which nets cash against short debt only, it identifies whether cash matters as a debt offset or as a general shock absorber, and it finally tests a clean cash carrier after the gen-1 cash signal died from the ZSCORE(IND_RANK) construction bug rather than from economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginCushionAgainstHardClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: What lets a firm survive maturing hard claims is the cushion between price and cost: a high gross margin means demand or input shocks can be absorbed before the firm turns cash-negative, whereas a low-margin firm with the same asset-scaled profitability is one shock away from being unable to service claims.
evaluated.reasoning: Gross margin (gp/sale) is not a smoothed version of asset-scaled profitability (gp/at) but its orthogonal factor — the two differ by asset turnover — so this adjudicates whether the interaction runs through pricing-power cushion or capital productivity, a question the archive has never separated. Together with the accepted revenue-scale control it completes a clean decomposition of the winning coverage effect into margin, turnover and scale components, using only high-coverage items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ClaimSizeAndHardnessVersusProfit
evaluated.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lct), RATIO(lct, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Near-term claim risk has two separate dimensions — how *hard* the maturing claims are (bank debt versus trade credit) and how *large* they are relative to the firm — and profitability must be compared against both; a profitable firm with a small, mostly-soft claim book is genuinely safe, while claim hardness alone understates risk for firms whose current book is enormous.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best joint result is the rank difference between gross profitability and hard-claim share (fmb 4.82, α +3.6%), but claim *intensity* has only ever appeared as a modulator, where it performed badly for portfolio-composition reasons; putting it inside the ranked distress side instead tests whether the two claim dimensions are complements. Both inputs are bounded ranks, so this should preserve the strong cross-sectional slope rather than reintroducing skew.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TroughOperatingIncomeOverClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: Refinancing capacity is judged by what happens in the firm's worst year: a firm whose five-year minimum operating income — after depreciation, and frequently negative — still covers a meaningful share of claims coming due has demonstrated it can survive a downturn without external funding, and this demonstrated resilience is priced slowly.
evaluated.reasoning: The earlier trough proposal was rightly criticized because gross profit is almost never negative, making its minimum a lagged level; oiadp does go negative for roughly a quarter of firm-years, so its five-year minimum is a genuine downside-state variable and the ratio distinguishes firms that fell into loss from those that never did. This is the only surviving way to bring realized downside risk into the near-term-claim frame that has produced the archive's best results.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitRankVersusNetHardClaimRank
evaluated.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash extinguishes maturing debt, so the distress side of the profitability comparison should be hard claims *net* of cash; ranking that net measure prevents cash-rich outliers from dominating while preserving the economic content that a firm holding cash against its short debt bears no rollover risk.
evaluated.reasoning: NetHardClaimShareAgainstProfit delivered α +4.5% (t 3.81) with FMB −1.25, the same skew signature as the other cash-based carrier, so this places the identical economic quantity inside the rank-difference structure that produced the archive's best cross-sectional evidence. Comparing it against Signal 2 also separates whether cash is best treated as a debt offset or as a standalone liquidity buffer, which is the remaining open question in this family before the final generation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashSubstitutesForWeakProfit
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquidity and earning power are substitutes in avoiding forced refinancing: for firms with weak gross profitability, cash held against maturing claims is the only thing standing between them and distressed funding, so it should be priced there, whereas for highly profitable firms the operating flow already covers the claim book and idle cash adds little.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a true conditional rather than the additive blend the critic rejected, and it tests the substitution quadrant that the archive has never evaluated cleanly — the gen-1 attempt died from the ZSCORE(IND_RANK) construction bug, and gen-6 tested only the complementary version (cash weighted by *high* profitability, α +4.4%, t 4.12). Winsorizing the cash ratio at 5% directly addresses the skew that produced the negative FMB slopes in both prior cash-carrier signals, so the two metrics have a chance to align.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkSafetyScore
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival is governed by the binding constraint, not by an average: a firm is only as safe as its weaker dimension, so a highly profitable firm with hard maturing debt and an unprofitable firm with soft claims should both be classified as risky, and only firms strong on *both* dimensions should command the safety premium.
evaluated.reasoning: A minimum is not a monotone transform of either the sum or the product — it is a non-smooth aggregator that deliberately refuses to let strength on one dimension compensate for weakness on the other — so it makes a distinct economic claim about how distress risk aggregates rather than restating the archived product with a different standardization. Comparing it against the additive rank difference (fmb 4.82, α +3.6%) and the centered-carrier product (fmb 4.15, α +4.0%) tells us whether the mechanism is compensatory or constraint-driven, which is the substantive question behind all three forms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UncoveredShareOfMaturingClaims
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the *fraction* of claims coming due that the firm cannot meet from cash on hand plus a year of gross profit; that uncovered share measures dependence on external funding directly and is comparable across firm sizes and industries.
evaluated.reasoning: The denominator is now current liabilities, which is strictly positive, so the sign-inverting non-monotonicity the critic identified in the profit-deflated version disappears and the signal is bounded above at one and monotone in the shortfall. It is not the reciprocal of GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims because cash enters the numerator and the measure is a coverage *deficit share* rather than a coverage multiple, and it should sharpen the FMB slope that the asset-scaled shortfall version (α −5.7%, t −4.26, fmb only −1.14) left weak.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkNetOfCash
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is only as safe as its weaker dimension, and the correct measure of the claim dimension is hard maturing debt *net of the cash that can extinguish it*; a firm that is profitable and whose cash already covers its short debt has no binding constraint, while failing either test leaves it exposed.
evaluated.reasoning: This unites the two independently validated gen-7 improvements — the weakest-link aggregator (best fmb 4.91 and Sharpe 0.333) and the cash-netted hard-claim rank (best alpha +5.3%, t 4.76) — each of which improved a different metric relative to the parent design, so the combination targets joint strength rather than one dimension. Both legs are bounded industry ranks, so the skew that broke the FMB slopes of raw cash carriers cannot reappear, and coverage should hold at ≈0.124.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TripleConstraintSafety
evaluated.expression: MIN(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival requires earning power, soft maturing claims, and a liquid reserve simultaneously; if any one of the three is weak the firm is exposed regardless of the other two, so the safety premium should accrue only to firms clearing all three constraints.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows all three ingredients matter separately, but nothing tells us how many constraints must bind at once; adding cash coverage as a third weakest-link component answers that and directly tests whether the top decile becomes more sharply defined (higher alpha) or merely narrower and noisier (lower t-stat). It is the natural next step from Signal 1 and its comparison with it is the informative part.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TighteningBindingConstraint
evaluated.hypothesis: What is priced slowly is not only the level of a firm's binding safety constraint but its movement: a firm whose weakest dimension is deteriorating — earnings slipping relative to peers, or maturing hard claims rising — is migrating toward distress, and the market reacts to the reported level rather than to the direction of the constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a genuinely new construct rather than a re-parameterization: it converts the archive's best static score into a state *change*, testing whether the mispricing is about mislevelled safety or about slow updating on deteriorating safety. Because the underlying score is bounded in [0,1], its annual change is well-behaved without winsorization, and coverage costs only one extra lag.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkOnDebtIntensity
evaluated.hypothesis: If the binding claim constraint is the *quantity* of maturing debt relative to the firm rather than its share of the current book, then scaling short debt by assets should preserve or improve the weakest-link result while covering firms whose current liabilities are small or unreported.
evaluated.reasoning: The two claim measures have never been compared inside the weakest-link structure, and dlc/at was the carrier with the archive's widest coverage (0.144 versus 0.125), so this simultaneously tests the economic question and the robustness of the leading result to a broader sample. A materially higher coverage with comparable statistics would make this the preferred final specification.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DownsideProfitWeakestLink
evaluated.hypothesis: The profitability constraint binds in bad years, not average ones, so the relevant earning-power leg of a binding-constraint safety score is the firm's worst recent operating income; a firm whose trough profitability is still healthy and whose maturing claims are mostly soft has no state in which it is forced to the credit market.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the arithmetic complement of the leading signal with a genuine candidate that keeps the validated weakest-link aggregator but upgrades the profitability leg from a current-year level to a realized downside state, which oiadp can express because it goes negative for a substantial share of firm-years. It also gives the trough concept a fair test inside the structure that works, after the ratio form (TroughOperatingIncomeOverClaims) failed at α −0.7% while the same trough idea in the total-liability frame had earlier scored fmb 2.61.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SafetyScoreWhereHistoryLooksBad
evaluated.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors classify firms with accumulated retained-earnings deficits as chronic distress cases and do not differentiate among them, so the binding-constraint safety score should carry the most information exactly there — a deficit firm that is profitable and free of hard maturing claims is far safer than its loss history implies, while a deficit firm failing either constraint deserves its discount.
evaluated.reasoning: This respects the direction the archive actually established — the profitability premium is *larger* where retained earnings are low (ProfitPremiumInDeficitFirms fmb 3.36, α +2.7%, Sharpe 0.280) — rather than going long high-RE firms as the flagged version mistakenly did, and it is therefore not an Altman-score rediscovery. It asks the one remaining structural question worth a slot before the final generation: whether the archive's two independent channels compose as a state-contingent amplification, with the non-negative deficit modulator muting firms whose earnings history already reassures the market.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetCurrentClaimWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(lct, che), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: If what binds is the total settlement obligation coming due within the year rather than only its hard bank-debt component, then all current liabilities net of cash should be the correct claim leg, since payables and accruals must also ultimately be funded from operations.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive established that *near-term* claims dominate total leverage, but never resolved whether hardness (dlc) or the full current book (lct) is the binding measure once cash is netted out — the hard-versus-soft test was run only in the multiplicative form. Holding the aggregator, the profitability leg and the asset scaler fixed makes this a clean one-variable adjudication of the central economic claim of the whole research line.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BottomLineProfitWeakestLink
evaluated.hypothesis: If the profitability leg of the safety score works because it measures genuine debt-servicing capacity rather than because gross profitability is a known return predictor, then replacing gross profit with operating income after depreciation — a measure net of overhead and capital consumption — should preserve or improve the result.
evaluated.reasoning: Every strong signal in the archive uses revt−cogs, so the finding is vulnerable to the charge that it is Novy-Marx gross profitability wearing a distress costume; oiadp is economically the cash claim-servicing measure and is only weakly correlated with gross profit in the cross-section. The trough version of oiadp inside this aggregator already produced fmb 3.10 and α +3.1%, so the current-level version is the natural and final robustness test of the profitability leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginAsThirdBindingConstraint
evaluated.expression: MIN(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival requires earning power, soft maturing claims, and a pricing cushion: a firm with thin margins converts any cost or demand shock straight into a funding shortfall, so the margin should act as a third constraint that binds independently of asset-scaled profitability and claim structure.
evaluated.reasoning: Adding cash as a third constraint kept the alpha at +5.2% with a t of 4.74, showing the aggregator tolerates a third leg; margin is the more orthogonal candidate because gp/at equals margin times asset turnover, and the margin channel independently produced α +3.6% (t 3.59) in the product form. This tests whether the pricing cushion adds a genuinely separate binding dimension or merely narrows the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TotalNetDebtWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The alternative to the near-term thesis is that total net indebtedness is what binds against earning power, with maturity structure irrelevant once cash is netted out; under that view long-term debt is an equally hard claim because it must eventually be refinanced.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the decisive falsification test for the thesis that has driven the last five generations — that *short-dated* claims, not total leverage, are what interact with profitability — because it changes only the maturity content of the claim leg while holding the aggregator, cash-netting, scaler and profitability leg identical to Signal 1. A materially weaker result confirms the near-term mechanism; a comparable result would mean the discovery is about net indebtedness generally, which is important to know before reporting the final specification.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtServiceWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dlc, xint), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What creditors actually demand each year is maturing principal *plus* interest, so the binding claim constraint is the total annual debt-service call on the firm rather than a stock of short debt; a firm whose earning power is strong and whose yearly service demand is small has no constraint that binds, while a high service call makes even profitable firms dependent on credit markets.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the economic content of the claim leg from a balance-sheet stock to a cash-service flow — adding the interest component, which embeds the price lenders charge and has never appeared inside the weakest-link aggregator — so the outcome is not predictable from the cash-netting or asset-scaling parents. It also revives the credit-cost channel (LenderRateVersusReportedProfit, α +1.6%, t 1.98) in the structure that has proven able to convert weak channels into strong ones, at coverage comparable to the dlc/at family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PeakShortDebtRelianceWeakestLink
evaluated.hypothesis: Fiscal-year-end balance sheets understate true funding practice because firms pay down revolvers before the reporting date; the firm's *peak* short-debt reliance over the past three years reveals how hard it actually leans on the short end, and only firms that have never leaned hard, and are profitable, are genuinely unconstrained.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the lagged-score duration idea, a three-year maximum of the claim ratio is not close to a monotone transform of its current value — it is precisely the firms whose current snapshot looks clean but whose history does not that get reclassified, which is where the measurement error in short-debt reporting lives. It keeps the validated aggregator and profitability leg fixed so the test isolates snapshot-versus-peak measurement of the binding claim, at a coverage cost of only two extra years of history.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: LeveredTurnaroundTrend
considered.hypothesis: An improving operating profitability trajectory is most valuable — and most underappreciated — for highly levered firms, where a rising trend mechanically reduces default probability and transfers value from creditors to equity; the same trend in an unlevered firm carries little option value.
considered.reasoning: TREND over five years captures the direction of the profitability state rather than its level, which is the variable that resolves distress uncertainty, and the leverage rank scales the payoff so that deteriorating levered firms sit at the short end. This is a genuine interaction because the trend's return relevance is conditioned on the distress state, not on profitability alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LeverageWeightedGrossProfit
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, ADD(cogs, xsga)), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: Because equity is a residual claim, one unit of operating profitability moves equity value far more when the firm carries heavy liabilities and a thin working-capital buffer; investors underreact to this leverage-amplified information, so profitability earns its largest premium exactly where distress exposure is greatest.
considered.reasoning: The critique was that a z-scored leverage multiplier flips sign for low-leverage firms and pooled unprofitable-unlevered names into the long leg; replacing it with a strictly non-negative distress weight (rank of a leverage plus working-capital-deficiency composite in [0,1]) makes the signal monotone in profitability at every leverage level and near zero for the safest firms. The long leg is therefore unambiguously profitable-and-stressed and the short leg unprofitable-and-stressed, which is the interaction the hypothesis describes rather than either main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorstCaseObligationCoverage
considered.hypothesis: Default is triggered by the trough of operating earnings, not their average, so the distress-relevant quantity is the firm's worst recent operating profit relative to its total obligations; markets extrapolate mean profitability and therefore underprice firms whose downside profitability still covers their liability stock.
considered.reasoning: This is no longer the inverse of net-debt/EBITDA: the numerator is a left-tail (three-year minimum) profitability state rather than a level or smoothed mean, which is a genuinely distress-conditioned way of measuring profitability. Scaling by total liabilities instead of interest-bearing debt removes the exploding-denominator fragility for zero-debt firms, since every firm has non-trivial liabilities, so winsorization is a mild guard rather than the source of the signal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeficitFirmCashProfit
considered.hypothesis: Firms with accumulated retained-earnings deficits are tarred by their loss history and priced as chronic distress cases; among these firms current cash profitability is the variable that actually resolves survival, and it is systematically undervalued relative to firms whose long earnings record already reassures investors.
considered.reasoning: The critique was that rank-summing cash profitability, leverage and retained earnings simply re-assembles known Altman/Ohlson and cash-profitability components additively; this version instead multiplies signed cash profitability by a non-negative accumulated-deficit weight, so the payoff exists only through the interaction and vanishes for firms with large retained earnings. It uses the cumulative-profitability distress channel as a state variable rather than as an additive return predictor, and is distinct from Signal 1 by conditioning on earnings history rather than on current balance-sheet leverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderRefinancingPressure
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lt)))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that must roll over debt within the year and hold little cash have the strongest incentive to report non-cash earnings to preserve covenant headroom and credit terms; such accrual-supported profits reverse, while cash-backed profits at the same refinancing pressure signal genuine solvency.
considered.reasoning: The conditioning variable is now near-term maturity pressure (short-term debt share net of cash holdings), a maturity-structure distress dimension distinct from the leverage level that drives the standard accrual anomaly. Industry-standardizing the accrual component makes the measure two-sided, so the long leg holds cash-backed earners under refinancing pressure and the short leg holds accrual-inflated ones, eliminating the one-sided pooling of low-leverage names the critic identified.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DistressPricedWhereProfitWeak
considered.expression: MUL(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at))))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(pi, at), 2))))
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet distress is priced only when profitability cannot service it: among firms with weak or negative pretax income, leverage and working-capital deficiency forecast real insolvency and low returns, while firms with weak earnings but clean balance sheets are cheap survivors that recover.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the loss indicator with a continuous rank of two-year average unprofitability removes the mass point at zero that degenerated the portfolio breakpoints, so every firm receives a distinct score and coverage stays full. The signed carrier here is the distress composite scaled by a smooth weakness weight — the mirror image of Signal 1 — so it tests whether distress pricing strengthens as profitability fades rather than re-labelling the known loss-firm effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OperatingFinancialDoubleLeverage
considered.hypothesis: Fixed-cost intensity (depreciation per unit of sales) amplifies the earnings sensitivity of a downturn, and when it is stacked on top of financial leverage the compounded operating-plus-financial risk is systematically underestimated, so double-levered firms subsequently underperform.
considered.reasoning: This tests the cost-structure side of profitability rather than its level, giving an interaction the archive has not touched: the same debt load is much more dangerous for a firm whose margins cannot flex. The signed industry-rank z-score for operating leverage keeps both legs populated (capital-light levered firms are long, capital-heavy levered firms are short) and the leverage rank mutes debt-free firms where operating leverage is not a distress channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FlowVersusStockSolvencyGap
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet leverage and earnings-based interest coverage classify distress differently, and investors (like credit screens and index filters) anchor on the visible stock measure; firms that look highly levered but whose operating profit easily services their interest burden are misclassified as risky and are therefore underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the profitability × leverage-rank product family entirely and instead prices the *disagreement* between a flow-based (profit-to-interest) and a stock-based (liabilities-to-assets) distress classification, which is neither the gross-profitability premium nor a leverage sort. Both channels enter as bounded industry ranks so the long leg is coherently "levered but comfortably covered" and the short leg is "low-book-leverage but interest-strained," with neither theme able to drive the spread alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ObligationGrowthOutpacingProfit
considered.hypothesis: Distress is built, not inherited: when a firm's liabilities expand faster than its operating earning power, the incremental obligations are not self-financing and future default risk rises, yet the market treats liability-funded expansion as growth rather than as deteriorating solvency capacity.
considered.reasoning: Rather than swapping the denominator of the archived coverage ratio, this compares the *flows* of the two themes — asset-scaled liability accumulation versus asset-scaled profit accumulation — so the signal is high only when obligations grow without matching profit support, an imbalance neither a leverage level nor a profit-change sort captures. Using asset-scaled first differences instead of growth rates avoids the exploding ratios that plague GROWTH(oibdp) for firms with near-zero or negative base earnings.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashRunwayForWeakEarners
considered.hypothesis: Liquidity buffers are priced asymmetrically: for firms with weak operating profitability, cash relative to total liabilities is the survival runway that determines whether distress is realized, whereas for already-profitable firms the same cash is idle balance-sheet slack that earns no premium and may signal agency costs.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the trivial ΔROA-to-liabilities idea with a genuine state-contingent liquidity mechanism, testing whether the cash cushion offsets weak profitability — the "offsets" leg of the task's economic story that the archive has not probed. The profitability term is a centered bounded rank z-score, so the long leg is weak-earner/high-cash and the short leg is strong-earner/high-cash, with cash-poor firms concentrated near zero rather than at an extreme.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CenteredEarningsRiskUnderLeverage
considered.hypothesis: Default probability is driven by the product of cash-flow volatility and obligation size, so among levered firms earnings instability should be penalized sharply while among unlevered firms it should be nearly irrelevant; the market applies a roughly uniform volatility discount and therefore misprices the interaction.
considered.reasoning: The critique was correct that a non-negative VOL times a non-negative leverage rank, then negated, ranks unlevered firms at the top; centering the volatility input as an industry-rank z-score fixes the ordering so that stable levered firms occupy the long leg, volatile levered firms the short leg, and debt-free firms sit in the middle. This makes the tested quantity the leverage-conditional slope on earnings risk rather than the level of earnings volatility itself.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OverheadRetrenchmentUnderDebt
considered.hypothesis: Levered firms have no slack to absorb rising overhead: a falling SG&A-to-sales ratio credibly restores debt-service capacity and lowers default risk, while overhead creep at a levered firm is an early, under-monitored sign of margin erosion that will meet a hard obligation constraint.
considered.reasoning: This swaps the discredited book-tax-difference channel for a cost-discipline channel: the change in overhead intensity is only distress-relevant when obligations are large, which is a conditioning claim rather than a restatement of any cost-stickiness or profitability anomaly. The centered rank z-score of the overhead change keeps both legs populated among levered firms and mutes debt-free firms, where SG&A drift carries no solvency implication.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LenderRateVersusReportedProfit
considered.hypothesis: The effective interest rate a firm pays embeds private lender information about default risk; when accounting profitability looks healthy, equity investors are complacent and ignore this credit-market warning, so a high lender-imposed rate predicts low returns most strongly among apparently profitable firms.
considered.reasoning: This introduces an external, price-based distress measure rather than another balance-sheet ratio, and conditions it on profitability, so the tested claim is that credit-market and accounting signals conflict and the credit market wins. The signed carrier is the industry-standardized borrowing rate (raw-ratio IND_ZSCORE, which evaluates reliably) while the non-negative profitability rank mutes unprofitable firms, where the equity market is already alert to distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SolvencyMarginOwnHistoryPosition
considered.hypothesis: Credit quality is judged relative to a firm's own history: when operating profit per unit of obligations sits near the top of its five-year range, default risk has fallen materially from the level embedded in prices, and this within-firm improvement is absorbed more slowly than the cross-sectional level.
considered.reasoning: This changes the reference frame rather than the ingredients — position in own history instead of position in the cross-section — which separates firm-specific credit-quality improvement from persistent industry or size effects that a cross-sectional coverage sort inherits. It is parsimonious, uses only oibdp and lt so coverage should exceed the TS_MIN-based winner, and provides a clean read on whether the coverage effect is a level or a within-firm-change phenomenon.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsDrawdownUnderObligations
considered.hypothesis: Distance below peak earning power measures proximity to covenant breach and refinancing failure, and this drawdown is dangerous only when obligations are large; markets extrapolate the current earnings level and underweight how far a levered firm has fallen from the cash-flow base its debt was raised against.
considered.reasoning: Peak-to-current earnings drawdown is a distinct temporal concept from the archive's trend and level signals — it captures crisis proximity rather than direction or average — and interacting it with leverage is exactly the state dependence the mandate asks for. Centering the drawdown with IND_ZSCORE (not a non-negative magnitude) fixes the ordering flaw the critic identified in gen 1, so at-peak levered firms are long, deeply drawn-down levered firms are short, and debt-free firms sit near the middle.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginCompressionUnderObligations
considered.hypothesis: Rising unit cost of sales erodes the cash flow pledged against fixed claims, so gross-margin compression is a leading indicator of default risk only for obligation-heavy firms; the market reads margin drift as an operating detail and misses its solvency implication where there is no slack to absorb it.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the net-debt-issuance-adjacent flow diagnostic with a cost-side margin channel that no archived signal touches, and it conditions on obligations rather than adding another debt-growth leg. The signed carrier is the centered change in cost intensity and the weight is a non-negative leverage rank, so improving-margin levered firms are long, compressing-margin levered firms are short, and debt-free firms sit near the middle; coverage should be high since only cogs, sale, lt and at are required.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CurrentProfitVersusLossHistory
considered.hypothesis: Investors anchor distress assessments on a firm's accumulated earnings record — the retained-earnings deficit that credit models weight heavily — and are slow to recognize when current operating profitability has already recovered; the gap between present earning power and the accumulated record is therefore underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This is a new economic claim rather than a blend of archived signals: it prices the *disagreement between stock and flow measures of profitability*, where the stock version (retained earnings to assets) is the classic accumulated-distress state variable and the flow version is current earning power. The rank-difference structure has evaluated cleanly in this environment, keeps both legs populated (long = recovering deficit firms, short = firms coasting on past earnings with weak current profit), and requires only oibdp, re and at so coverage should exceed the TS_MIN family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FloatFinancedProfitability
considered.hypothesis: Negative working capital is a standard distress marker, but for firms with strong gross margins it instead reflects supplier and customer float — a cheap, self-renewing funding source — so the market over-penalizes working-capital deficiency among profitable firms and those firms subsequently outperform.
considered.reasoning: Rather than re-proposing cash-versus-profitability, this tests the opposite sign convention on a different distress dimension: whether profitability *reinterprets* a liquidity-deficiency signal instead of merely offsetting it. The centered working-capital carrier and non-negative gross-profitability weight put float-financed profitable operators in the long leg and working-capital-heavy profitable firms in the short leg, while unprofitable firms — where the deficiency is genuine distress — are muted near zero.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RolloverPressureAgainstProfit
considered.hypothesis: If the working-capital result is really about near-term funding risk, the active ingredient should be current debt rather than the full act−lct netting: profitable firms carrying heavy short-maturity debt must repeatedly return to credit markets, and that rollover exposure is not compensated in equity prices.
considered.reasoning: This decomposes Signal 1's mechanism by isolating the maturity-structure component of the liability side, so the pair jointly identifies whether the effect is a liquid-asset buffer story or a short-term-obligation story — an attribution the archive cannot currently make. The construction (centered distress carrier × non-negative profitability rank) is the one that has evaluated cleanly and keeps unprofitable firms muted, where rollover risk is already visibly priced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DebtServiceableCashAfterWorkingCapital
considered.hypothesis: Operating profit overstates the cash actually available to service obligations because growth in working capital absorbs it; the distress-relevant quantity is profit net of working-capital investment relative to total liabilities, and firms whose reported profitability is not truly available for debt service are overvalued.

It uses only oibdp, wcap and lt, so coverage should match or exceed the TS_MIN-based winner while adding a cash-conversion dimension the archive lacks.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ReplacementBurdenOnLeveredEarnings
considered.hypothesis: EBITDA overstates the cash genuinely available to service fixed claims when a large fraction of it must be reinvested to replace depreciating assets; for obligation-heavy firms this replacement burden is a hidden claim ahead of debt service, so levered firms whose earnings are mostly depreciation charges are riskier than their coverage ratios suggest.

The centered, winsorized carrier keeps both legs populated among levered firms (long = low replacement burden, short = depreciation-heavy) and mutes debt-free firms; it needs only dp, oibdp, lt and at, all high-coverage items.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CostRigidityUnderObligations
considered.hypothesis: A cost base dominated by fixed overhead rather than variable production cost cannot be shrunk when demand falls, so overhead-rigid firms convert a revenue shock into a solvency event; this fragility matters only when obligations are large, and the market prices cost structure as an operating characteristic rather than a distress amplifier.

Among levered firms the long leg is variable-cost-flexible operators and the short leg is overhead-rigid ones, with unlevered firms muted where cost rigidity carries no default implication.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DebtServiceEscalationVersusProfit
considered.hypothesis: The binding constraint is the cash interest claim, not the balance-sheet stock: when interest expense grows faster than operating profit — because of new borrowing, repricing, or the loss of cheap fixed-rate debt — the fixed-charge burden is escalating against a shrinking cushion, and equity holders bear the residual.

It keeps the rank-difference structure that has evaluated cleanly and that produced the archive's strongest t-stat, while making the economic claim about escalating fixed charges relative to earning power.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ReturnMinusBorrowingCostSpread
considered.hypothesis: Solvency dynamics are governed by whether a firm's operating return exceeds the rate its lenders charge: a positive spread makes leverage self-liquidating and default risk mean-reverting downward, while a negative spread means debt compounds faster than earnings, and the market does not fully impound this comparison.

The rank-difference form bounds the badly behaved low-debt tail of the borrowing-rate ratio (further winsorized) and keeps both legs economically interpretable: long = earns more than it pays, short = pays more than it earns.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaturityMixAgainstProfit
considered.expression: MUL(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: What makes profitability valuable is not the amount of debt but how soon it must be repaid: profitable firms that have termed out their borrowing are insulated from credit-market closures, while profitable firms funding themselves at the short end are exposed to rollover risk that equity prices do not discount.

If the maturity-share version retains the fmb ≈ 3.9 / alpha ≈ 4% profile, the mechanism is genuinely refinancing risk; if it collapses, the winner was about debt quantity and the modulator was doing the work.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims
considered.hypothesis: Solvency at the relevant horizon is whether one year of gross profit can retire the claims that actually come due; firms whose near-term obligations are small relative to their gross profit flow face negligible refinancing risk and are underpriced relative to that safety.

It is parsimonious, uses only revt, cogs and lct, and its comparison with Signal 1 pins down whether the effect is coverage-level or conditional-slope in nature.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RolloverShockAgainstProfit
considered.hypothesis: A profitable firm that is suddenly shifting its funding to the short end is being rationed by long-term lenders, so the *increase* in current-debt intensity is a live warning of financing stress that the market reads as ordinary working-capital borrowing.
considered.reasoning: This changes the winner from a state to a flow, which distinguishes a persistent capital-structure characteristic (possibly a risk-premium story spanned by known maturity effects) from a genuine news-based mispricing about deteriorating credit access. The design is deliberately identical in every other respect so the level-versus-change comparison is clean, and coverage should be close to 0.14 since only one lag is added.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RepairedEarningsRiskUnderObligations
considered.hypothesis: Default probability rises with the product of cash-flow volatility and obligation size, so earnings instability should be penalized sharply among obligation-heavy firms and be nearly irrelevant for debt-light firms; a market that applies a uniform volatility discount misprices this interaction.

Written with IND_ZSCORE of the raw volatility it should evaluate at coverage comparable to the other five-year-window signals (≈0.12–0.14), with stable levered earners long and volatile levered earners short.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitPremiumInDeficitFirms
considered.hypothesis: Firms carrying accumulated retained-earnings deficits are priced as chronic distress cases regardless of current performance, so the operating-profitability premium should be strongest exactly there, where profitability is the variable that resolves survival, and weakest among firms whose long earnings record already reassures investors.

It uses only oibdp, re and at, so coverage should stay near 0.14, and it delivers a lesson that none of the rollover-family signals in this batch can provide.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OperatingCycleVelocityUnderNearTermClaims
considered.hypothesis: A firm meets claims that come due out of the cash its operating cycle throws off, so the speed at which current assets convert into cash — cost of goods sold per dollar of current assets — is distress insurance precisely for firms whose balance sheets are loaded with near-term liabilities; slow-turning inventory and receivables cannot be converted on demand, making an otherwise identical claim load far more dangerous.

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HardVersusSoftNearTermClaims
considered.hypothesis: Not all claims due within a year are equally dangerous: bank and market debt is a hard claim whose non-payment triggers default, whereas payables and accruals are soft claims that roll with ongoing supplier relationships, so for profitable firms it is the *hardness* of near-term claims, not their quantity, that determines true distress risk.

If hardness is what matters, this should match or beat the winner; if the effect is really about total near-term claim size, it will weaken, which is itself decisive information for the remaining generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RolloverRiskAtHighCreditCost
considered.hypothesis: Short-maturity debt is dangerous in proportion to how expensive the firm's marginal credit already is: when lenders charge a high effective rate they are signalling limited willingness to refinance, so rollover exposure and a high borrowing cost compound into genuine default risk, whereas cheap borrowers can roll short debt at will.
